concepts.title: 2.5.2 Attractiveness of Industry
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 (appears only as the second half of five-forces answers)
understand: ==**The industry analysis culminates into identification of various issues and draws conclusions about the relative attractiveness or unattractiveness of the industry, both near-term and long-term.**== Strategists assess the industry outlook carefully, deciding whether industry and competitive conditions present an **attractive business opportunity** or whether growth and profit prospects are **gloomy**. This matters because companies invest capital — either the promoters' or from the public — and **should be inherently careful in choosing an industry**.
**The nine factors on which management may base such conclusions:**
**(i)** The industry's **growth potential** — is it futuristically viable?
**(ii)** Whether **competition currently permits adequate profitability**, and whether competitive forces will become **stronger or weaker**.
**(iii)** Whether industry profitability will be **favourably or unfavourably affected by the prevailing driving forces**.

**(iv)** The **competitive position of the organisation** in the industry and whether that position is likely to grow stronger or weaker. ICAI's parenthesis is important: ==being a **well-entrenched leader or strongly positioned contender in an otherwise lacklustre industry can still produce good profitability**; however, having to **fight an uphill battle against much stronger rivals can make an otherwise attractive industry unattractive**.==
**(v)** The **potential to capitalise on the vulnerabilities of weaker rivals** — perhaps converting an unattractive industry situation into a potentially rewarding company opportunity.
**(vi)** Whether the company is **able to defend against or counteract the factors** that make the industry unattractive.
**(vii)** The **degrees of risk and uncertainty** in the industry's future.
**(viii)** The **severity of problems confronting the industry as a whole**.
**(ix)** Whether **continued participation in this industry adds importantly to the firm's ability to be successful in other industries** in which it may have business interests.

**The general proposition and its qualification.** As a general proposition, ==if an industry's overall profit prospects are **above average**, the industry can be considered **attractive**; if below average, it is **unattractive**. However, **it is a mistake to think of industries as being attractive or unattractive to all firms in the industry and all potential entrants** — **attractiveness is relative, not absolute.** Industry environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong competitors.==

**What follows from the verdict.** An assessment that the industry is **fundamentally attractive** typically suggests that current participants employ strategies calculated to **strengthen their long-term competitive positions**, expanding sales efforts and investing in additional facilities and equipment as needed.

If the industry and competitive situation is judged **relatively unattractive**, more successful participants may choose to **invest cautiously**, look for ways to **protect their long-term competitiveness and profitability**, and perhaps **acquire smaller firms if the price is right**; over the longer term, strong companies may consider **diversification into more attractive businesses**.

**Weak companies in unattractive industries** may consider **merging with a rival to bolster market share and profitability** or, alternatively, **begin looking outside the industry for attractive diversification opportunities**.
concepts.example: Two firms look at the same slow-growing, price-competitive packaging industry. The entrenched leader with the lowest costs reads it as attractive and funds a new plant. A sub-scale follower reads the same industry as unattractive and merges with a rival to bolster share. Both readings are correct — that is what 'attractiveness is relative, not absolute' means.

inherent careful in choosing an industry
lacklustre industry can still produce good profitability

acquire smaller firms if the price is right
merging with a rival to bolster market share

memory.trick: Three strategic postures follow the verdict — **Strong firm + attractive industry** = expand and invest; **strong firm + unattractive industry** = invest cautiously, protect, buy cheap, then diversify; **weak firm + unattractive industry** = merge or leave.
key: Strengthen long-term positions; expand sales efforts; invest in facilities
Invest cautiously; protect competitiveness; acquire smaller firms if the price is right; later diversify
Merge with a rival to bolster share, or look outside the industry to diversify
memory.recall_trigger: Who is asking? Strong or weak — the industry's attractiveness depends on it

mistakes: Declaring an industry attractive or unattractive in the abstract. The study material insists attractiveness is relative to the firm asking the question.
Giving only the growth-potential factor. The published list has nine factors, and the firm's own competitive position is one of them.
Prescribing exit for every unattractive industry. Strong participants are told to invest cautiously, protect profitability and buy smaller firms cheaply before considering diversification.
Ignoring the near-term/long-term split. The conclusion must be drawn 'both near-term and long-term'.

🔗 SM Ch 4: the GE nine-cell matrix plots industry attractiveness against business strength, and the BCG matrix uses market growth
🔗 S02.16: a strong experience-curve position is what lets a leader profit in a lacklustre industry

approach: Open with the 'culminates… both near-term and long-term' sentence, give the nine factors as a numbered list, then the above-average/below-average proposition, then the relative-not-absolute qualification.
If the question is a case, finish with the posture that matches the firm's strength — expand, invest cautiously, or merge and look outside.

expected_questions.question: "Attractiveness is relative, not absolute." Explain how a strategist concludes on the attractiveness of an industry, and what strategies follow from the conclusion.
answer_points: Industry analysis culminates in conclusions about the relative attractiveness or unattractiveness of the industry, **both near-term and long-term**; companies invest the promoters' or the public's capital and should be careful in choosing an industry.

**The factors considered:** growth potential and futuristic viability; whether competition currently permits adequate profitability and whether the forces will strengthen or weaken; whether prevailing driving forces will affect profitability favourably or unfavourably; the firm's own competitive position and whether it will grow stronger or weaker; the potential to capitalise on the vulnerabilities of weaker rivals; the ability to defend against or counteract the unattractive factors; the degrees of risk and uncertainty; the severity of problems confronting the industry as a whole; and whether continued participation adds importantly to the firm's success in other industries.
**The general proposition:** above-average overall profit prospects make an industry attractive; below-average prospects make it unattractive.

**The qualification:** it is a mistake to think of industries as attractive or unattractive to all firms and all potential entrants — attractiveness is relative, not absolute. Environments unattractive to weak competitors may be attractive to strong ones; a well-entrenched leader in a lacklustre industry can still earn good profits, while an uphill battle against much stronger rivals can make an otherwise attractive industry unattractive.

**Strategies that follow:** if attractive, strengthen long-term competitive positions, expand sales efforts and invest in facilities. If unattractive, successful participants invest cautiously, protect long-term competitiveness and profitability, perhaps acquire smaller firms if the price is right, and over the longer term consider diversification. Weak companies in unattractive industries may merge with a rival to bolster market share and profitability, or look outside the industry for diversification opportunities.

Nine factors, including the firm's own competitive position and the ability to exploit weaker rivals.

Attractive → strengthen position, expand, invest. Unattractive and strong → invest cautiously, protect, buy small firms cheap, later diversify. Unattractive and weak → merge or look outside.

concepts.title: 2.5.3 Experience Curve
understand: ==**The experience curve is akin to a learning curve, which explains the efficiency increase gained by workers through repetitive productive work.** The experience curve is based on the commonly observed phenomenon that **unit costs decline as a firm accumulates experience in terms of a cumulative volume of production**. It is based on the concept, **"we learn as we grow"**.==
==**The implication** is that **larger firms in an industry would tend to have lower unit costs as compared to those for smaller companies, thereby gaining a competitive cost advantage.**==

**The experience curve results from a variety of factors:** **learning effects, economies of scale, product redesign and technological improvements in production.** Note that economies of scale is only *one* of the four causes — the experience curve is not a synonym for scale economies.

**The three features of the experience curve:** **(i)** as business organisations grow, **they gain experience**; **(ii)** experience may provide an **advantage over the competition** — ==**experience is a key barrier to entry**==; **(iii)** **large and successful organisations possess a stronger "experience effect"**.

A typical experience curve is drawn with cumulative volume on one axis and unit cost on the other, falling steeply at first and then flattening. ==**As a business grows, it understands the complexities and benefits from its experiences.**==

**Relevance in strategic management.** The concept is relevant for a number of areas. **(i)** It is considered **a barrier for new firms contemplating entry** into an industry. **(ii)** It is **used to build market share and discourage competition.** **(iii)** ICAI's contemporary Indian illustration: ==**in the contemporary Indian automobile industry, the experience curve phenomenon seems to be working in Maruti Suzuki.**== **(iv)** For competitors facing an entrenched experience-curve leader, ==**the likely strategic choice can be a market niche approach or segmentation based on demography or geography.**==

Read this heading together with §2.5.1: 'economies of scale' is the second of the seven barriers to entry, and 'experience is a key barrier to entry' is the experience curve's own second feature — ICAI connects the two deliberately, which is why MTP September 2026 Series 2 offered the experience curve and the barriers to entry as alternatives to each other in one question.
concepts.example: Two cement plants start the same year. The one that has since produced four times the tonnage has retrained its crews, redesigned its kiln feed, bought bigger mills and automated packing — four of the four stated causes — and its cost per tonne is materially lower. A new entrant cannot buy that position; it can only pick a niche, such as a single state or a specialist grade. That is the experience curve both as a cost advantage and as a barrier to entry.
keywords: efficiency increase gained by workers through repetitive productive work
unit costs decline as a firm accumulates experience
learning effects, economies of scale, product redesign and technological improvements
experience is a key barrier to entry
build market share and discourage competition
market niche approach or segmentation based on demography or geography

memory.trick: Four causes = "L-E-P-T" ("Learn, Expand, Perfect, Technologise"): Learning effects, Economies of scale, Product redesign, Technological improvements. Three features = Grow → Advantage (barrier) → Bigger firms, stronger effect.

Omitting 'we learn as we grow'. It is the study material's own encapsulation and an easy keyword mark.

Forgetting the Maruti Suzuki illustration, which ICAI prints in the chapter and candidates can cite verbatim.

expected_questions.question: State the factors from which the experience curve results, and explain the strategic choice open to a competitor facing a firm that enjoys a strong experience-curve position.
answer_points: The experience curve results from a variety of factors: **learning effects, economies of scale, product redesign and technological improvements in production.**

Its features are that as organisations grow they gain experience; experience may provide an advantage over the competition and is a key barrier to entry; and large and successful organisations possess a stronger 'experience effect'.

The implication is that larger firms tend to have lower unit costs than smaller companies, gaining a competitive cost advantage; the concept is used to **build market share and discourage competition**, and ICAI cites **Maruti Suzuki** in the contemporary Indian automobile industry.

**The competitor's strategic choice:** facing such a firm, the likely choice is a **market niche approach, or segmentation based on demography or geography** — competing where the leader's accumulated volume advantage does not apply.
This is why the experience curve is treated as a barrier for new firms contemplating entry into an industry, alongside economies of scale in the list of seven barriers to entry.
keywords: segmentation based on demography or geography

official_questions.question: Which concept explains the efficiency increase gained by worker through repetitive production work, leading to cost reduction and competitive advantage? List down its relevance features in strategic management. (5 Marks)
answer_points: **The concept is Experience Curve.** The experience curve, akin to a learning curve, explains the efficiency increase gained by workers through repetitive productive work. concepts.title: 2.5.4 Value Creation
concepts.evidence: PYQ 0 · RTP 0 · MTP 0 — a heading added in the 2026 syllabus edition and not yet examined
understand: **The concept of value creation** was introduced primarily for providing products and services to customers **with more worth**. ==**Value is measured by a product's features, quality, availability, durability, performance and by its services, for which customers are willing to pay.**== The concept later took more space in business, and organisations started discussing **value creation for stakeholders**.

==**Value creation is an activity or performance by the firm to create value that increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or even the whole business system.**== Many businesses now focus on value creation both for **customers purchasing its products and services** and for **stakeholders in the business who want to see their investment appreciate in value**. Ultimately the concept gives a business a **competitive advantage in the industry** and helps it earn **above average profits/returns**.

**The profitable pricing band.** The chapter's figure sets out the arithmetic of value creation on a single vertical scale: at the bottom is the **firm's cost of value creation**; above it is the **price**; above that, the **value to customer**. The gap between price and cost is the **firm's margin**; the gap between value to customer and price is the **customer's surplus**; and the whole band between cost and value to customer is the **profitable pricing band**. ==**It is basically the value the consumer wants to pay, over and above the price that the business wants to charge from the consumer. This excess amount is called value creation, wherein the consumers value the product or service more than it actually costs them.**==

**Competitive advantage leads to superior profitability.** ==At the most basic level, how profitable a company becomes depends on **three factors**: **(1) the value customers place on the company's products; (2) the price that a company charges for its products; and (3) the costs of creating those products.**==

**Utility versus price.** The value customers place on a product reflects the **utility** they get from it — **the happiness or satisfaction gained from consuming or owning the product**. ==**Utility must be distinguished from price. Utility is something that customers get from a product**; it is a function of the attributes of the product, such as its **performance, design, quality, and point-of-sale and after-sale service**.==

**Porter's two routes.** Companies ultimately aim to achieve **sustainable competitive advantage**, which enables them to succeed in the long run. ==Michael Porter argues that a company can generate competitive advantage in **two different ways, either through differentiation or cost advantage**.== According to Porter, **differentiation means the capability to provide customers superior and special value in the form of a product's special features and quality, or in the form of after-sales customer service**. As a result of differentiation a company **can demand a higher price** for its products or services, and it will earn higher profits from differentiation **in case the expenses stay comparable to the costs of competitors**.

**Why the value chain follows.** Differentiation and cost advantage affect a company's ability to achieve competitive advantage, but **many different organisational functions influence whether a company can achieve either**. ==Michael Porter used the concept of the **value chain** to explore more closely the different functions of organisations and the mutual interactions among them: **value chain analysis provides an excellent tool to examine the origin of competitive advantage**, dividing the organisation into **two strategically important groups of activities — primary activities and supporting activities** — which help comprehend the **potential sources for differentiation** and understand an **organisation's cost behaviour**.==
concepts.example: A premium water purifier costs the maker ₹6,000, sells at ₹11,000, and a buyer who values the health benefit and the five-year service plan would have paid ₹14,000. The firm's margin is ₹5,000, the customer's surplus is ₹3,000, and the profitable pricing band runs from ₹6,000 to ₹14,000. The ₹3,000 the customer keeps is the value created — and it is what makes the purchase feel worth more than it cost.

increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or even the whole business system

memory.trick: Three profitability factors = **V-P-C** ("Value, Price, Cost"). Stack them bottom-up: **C**ost → **P**rice → **V**alue; margin sits between C and P, customer's surplus between P and V.
key: Value customers place on the product (utility: performance, design, quality, service)
Price minus cost — the firm's share
Value minus price — the customer's share
memory.recall_trigger: Cost, Price, Value — margin below, surplus above

mistakes: Equating value with price. The study material insists utility is something customers *get* from a product, and must be distinguished from price.
Naming four or five factors of profitability. There are **three**: value customers place on the product, the price charged, and the cost of creating it.
Giving three routes to competitive advantage. Porter's argument as quoted here is **two** — differentiation or cost advantage. (The generic-strategies treatment in Chapter 3 adds focus.)
Forgetting the condition on differentiation: higher profits follow **only if expenses stay comparable to competitors' costs**.
Treating value creation as a customer-only idea. The study material extends it to stakeholders who want their investment to appreciate.

expected_questions.question: Explain the concept of value creation. On what three factors does a company's profitability depend, and how does the study material distinguish utility from price?
answer_points: **Value creation** is an activity or performance by the firm to create value that increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or even the whole business system. It was introduced to provide products and services to customers with more worth, and value is measured by a product's features, quality, availability, durability, performance and services, for which customers are willing to pay.

Businesses now focus on value creation both for customers buying their products and for stakeholders who want their investment to appreciate; ultimately it gives competitive advantage in the industry and helps earn above-average profits or returns.

**The three factors on which profitability depends:** (1) the value customers place on the company's products; (2) the price the company charges for its products; and (3) the costs of creating those products.

**Utility versus price:** the value customers place on a product reflects the utility they get from it — the happiness or satisfaction gained from consuming or owning the product. Utility must be distinguished from price: utility is something customers *get* from a product, and is a function of the attributes of the product such as performance, design, quality and point-of-sale and after-sale service.

The gap between value to customer and price is the **customer's surplus**; between price and cost is the **firm's margin**; the whole band is the **profitable pricing band**. The excess of what the consumer would pay over the price charged is value creation — the consumer values the product more than it actually costs them.

recap: Value creation increases the worth of goods, services, business processes or the whole business system — for customers and for stakeholders.
Stack: cost of value creation → price → value to customer; margin below the price, customer's surplus above it, profitable pricing band across the whole.
Three profitability factors: value customers place on the product, price charged, cost of creating it.
Utility = happiness or satisfaction from consuming or owning; distinct from price; a function of performance, design, quality and service.
